\boxed{(p_1p_2\cdots p_r)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}}

**Derivation.**  
Write each number by its exponent vector $(i_1,\dots,i_r)\in\{0,\dots,n\}^r$. Since $\gcd$ and $\mathrm{lcm}$ act coordinatewise as $\min$ and $\max$, the game factorises across the $r$ primes. By symmetry under permuting the primes, the value under optimal play has the form $\prod_{j=1}^r p_j^{e}$ for a single exponent $e$.

Project onto one prime, say $p_1$. The projected multiset has size $N=(n+1)^r$ and contains each exponent $0,1,\dots,n$ exactly $m=(n+1)^{r-1}$ times. In the one-dimensional game on $a_1\le\dots\le a_N$ with Alice (min) moving first, induction shows Alice can force at most $a_{\lceil N/2\rceil}$ and Bob can force at least $a_{\lceil N/2\rceil}$: Alice always removes the current maximum via $\min$, Bob always removes the current minimum via $\max$. Hence the guaranteed exponent is the $\lceil N/2\rceil$-th smallest.

Because the sorted list consists of $m$ copies of each $0,\dots,n$,
$$\text{the }\Big\lceil\frac{(n+1)^r}{2}\Big\rceil\text{-th smallest exponent}
=\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\Big\rfloor.$$
Thus $e=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Alice can guarantee the final number is at most $\prod p_j^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, and Bob can force it to be at least that, so this is the minimal such $M$.
